problem_shape: This family is about systems that need help from data they are not allowed to freely collect, expose, or trust. Hospitals, phones, recommender services, browsers, sensor networks, blockchains, metro systems, and web domains all hold useful signals, but those signals can reveal people, business secrets, security weaknesses, or private training text. The shared real-world task is therefore not simply to learn a better model or audit a safer web service. It is to move useful evidence across organizational or device boundaries while keeping the dangerous parts hidden, and while assuming that some participants or attackers may lie, steal, poison, or infer what was meant to stay private. The 168 papers in this family circle the same pressure from different sides. Federated work keeps raw data local but must still combine learning. Privacy work adds noise, proofs, or partial sharing so outsiders cannot read sensitive details. Security work asks where sharing itself opens a door: stolen cookies, leaked model behavior, poisoned tools, attacked blockchains, exposed WebAssembly models, or side channels. The family exists because modern web intelligence is collaborative, but collaboration turns privacy and security from add-on features into the core engineering problem.
naive_failure: A smart beginner would keep private data on each device or organization, send only model updates or summary patterns to a shared server, and add a simple access rule saying who may participate. That is a reasonable first move because it avoids the most obvious leak: copying raw records into one database. It fails because summaries can still reveal details. The adapter-based federated language model attack shows that training updates can be worked backward into training text. Membership inference work shows that a model can betray whether a changed sentence was in its web training data. A second beginner move is to hide more information by adding noise, but too much noise makes the learned system less useful and unfairly weakens careful contributors. A third move is to trust participants, domains, tools, or validators once authenticated. The evidence shows why that breaks: clients can poison shared graph learning, subdomains can leak cookies, agents can be tricked by poisoned tools, and blockchain validators can collude.
mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is constrained sharing: decide exactly what useful signal may cross a boundary, what sensitive detail must be blocked, and how to check that the boundary was respected. In federated learning, the local holder keeps records and sends a shaped update, prototype, small adapter, or other summary. The central question is what that summary preserves. It should carry enough pattern to improve recommendations, graph clustering, fault diagnosis, metro forecasting, signal recovery, or multimodal learning, but not enough to reconstruct a person, sentence, sensor trace, or business dataset. Differential privacy is the noise version of this idea: deliberately blur each contribution so one record has limited visible effect, while preserving repeated patterns that appear across many records. Zero-knowledge proof systems are the verification version: prove that a rule was followed without revealing the private circuit, telemetry, identity credential, or simulation trace itself. Poisoning defenses and anomaly detectors are the trust version: compare incoming behavior against expected density, timing, memory, or update patterns and flag signals that look too strategically shaped. Incentive and blockchain papers add a payment and reputation layer, asking how to reward real contribution and punish free-riding. The tradeoff is useful cooperation versus leakage, verification versus cost, and privacy versus accuracy.
why_math_matters: The math matters because privacy and security failures are rarely visible in the raw surface of a system. A training update, browser module, cookie rule, blockchain action, or graph prototype may look harmless while carrying hidden information or hidden attack intent. The family needs measured constraints because hand-written promises such as share less, trust the server, or encrypt the channel do not answer the harder question: how much can an observer still infer after seeing the allowed output? Noise budgets matter because privacy is not all-or-nothing; every shared result spends some exposure, and DIARY treats recovery after unlearning as another place where exposure can be spent badly. Prototype alignment matters because clients may have different cluster counts or personal behavior patterns, so a single average can erase local structure. Density checks matter because poisoned graph updates may sit in strange regions compared with normal shared patterns. Formal proof systems matter because Blind-QEM, ZK-V, and USIM-less authentication need verifiable compliance without revealing the thing being checked. Security measurement also needs counting and comparison at scale: CookieDrift and Internet security indicators turn scattered weaknesses into measured exposure across domains. These tools exploit repeated structure while limiting what any single private case can reveal.
paper_family: The representative papers are siblings because each asks what can safely cross a boundary. Reconstructing Training Data from Adapter-based Federated Large Language Models and Decoding Web Memorization study the leak side: even when only updates or model behavior are visible, an attacker may infer hidden training text or membership. FeedGuard, RAFed, FedUMM, FedRMamba, federated signal recovery, and MF3 study the utility side: phones, sensors, transit systems, and multimodal clients need joint learning without centralizing records, so they pass selected updates, small adapters, or pattern summaries. FedCND, pFedDKS, Thorki, PAECL, prototype-aligned soft prompts, and verifiable federated recommendation show personalization pressure: clients are not copies of one another, so the system must separate shared structure from local needs. Poisoning and backdoor papers, including federated knowledge graph attacks and fairness-aware federated finance, treat collaboration as an attack surface where bad participants can bend the shared model. Xemis, WinFLoRA, DIARY, and the blockchain incentive paper focus on governance: noise, reward, rollback, and contribution scoring decide whether cooperation remains fair. Blind-QEM, ZK-V, USIM-less authentication, quantum-safe blockchain tutorials, and ZABAPAD move the same logic into cryptographic verification. Cookie theft, doxing, WebAssembly isolation, browser model obfuscation, selfish mining, tool poisoning, and RAG cost attacks widen the family beyond federated learning into web systems where hidden channels and strategic behavior turn sharing into risk.
what_changed: The 2026 version is broader and more adversarial than a simple private-training story. The evidence is dominated by WWW papers but also includes SIGIR, WSDM, and KDD, showing that privacy and security now touch search, recommendation, graph learning, language models, blockchains, browsers, and infrastructure measurement. The newer emphasis is on leakage after apparent protection: adapter updates leak text, semantic changes still reveal membership, recovery after unlearning creates another privacy phase, and outsourced quantum or driving verification must prove compliance without exposing the private object. Federated work is also becoming more personalized and heterogeneous. Papers handle different client data shapes, privacy choices, model sizes, cluster counts, modalities, and incentives instead of assuming one uniform client population.
limits: These papers assume the shared summaries, noise rules, proofs, measurements, or anomaly scores capture the real risk. That can fail when attackers adapt, when normal clients are highly unusual, or when side channels expose information outside the modeled boundary. Federated learning assumes local data holders are numerous or diverse enough that shared patterns are useful; sparse clients, extreme non-uniform data, or low-quality participants can weaken both accuracy and privacy. Noise-based protection assumes the privacy budget is calibrated to the setting, but the input evidence does not prove one setting transfers to another. Verification papers can prove a narrow rule while leaving surrounding software, incentives, or deployment choices vulnerable. Security measurement papers reveal exposure in studied domains or traces, not the full web.
